Loops

for iterates. The word after it is the mode — what kind of traversal this is — and it is required, so a loop always says what it walks.

ModeWalks
fromthe values of a collection
refthe keys of a table, or the indices of a list
rangea numeric range

Over values#

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let list<int> numeri ← [1, 2, 3]
    for from numeri let n {
        print n
    }
}

In lockstep#

from also walks several lists together. Join the sources with and (English and) and the binders the same way, and the loop walks them all in lockstep — one shared index, one value from each list per turn:

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let list<string> nomina ← ["Alia", "Brunus"]
    let list<int> aetates ← [34, 27]

    for from nomina and aetates at [i] let name and aetas {
        print i, name, aetas
    }
}

at (English at) names the shared index. The sources are listas, and the binders are plain names, one per source. The lists must have the same length: lengths known to differ are refused at check (`SEM010 itera_lockstep_length_mismatch`), and the walk never truncates to the shorter list. Maps and sets cannot be lockstep sources.

Since 1.19 a comma in a loop head means the next loop in, and every clause after it starts with its own from or range. The old comma series for from a, b is refused (PARSE001 itera_bare_comma_source). Nested comma clauses such as for range 0 ‥ m, range 0 ‥ n let i, j parse but are not lowered in 1.19 (SEM008 itera_nested_clause_unsupported): write two nested loops.

Over keys#

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let map<string, string> persona ← { "nomen": "Marcus", "urbs": "Roma" }
    for ref persona let clavis {
        print clavis, persona[clavis]
    }
}

The same mode gives you list indices, which is what you want when the position matters as much as the value:

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let list<int> numeri ← [10, 20, 30]
    for ref numeri let index {
        print index, numeri[index]
    }
}

Over a range#

‥ builds a range. The lower bound is included, the upper bound is not.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    for range 0 ‥ 3 let i {
        print i
    }
}

step sets the step:

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    for range 0 ‥ 10 step 2 let i {
        print i
    }
}

A range is also a value. Store it, print it, and walk it later; the English type word is range<int>.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let range<int> r ← 0 ‥ 3
    print r
    for range r let i {
        print i
    }
}

A stored range can carry a step, and the step is part of its type: let range<int, 2> evens ← 0…10 step 2 walks 0, 2, … 10, and evens.length() is 6. See ranges.

While#

while loops while a condition holds.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    mut int i ← 0
    while i ≺ 3 {
        i ← i + 1
        print i
    }
}

Leaving early#

break breaks out; continue skips to the next iteration.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let list<int> numeri ← [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    for from numeri let n {
        if n ≡ 2 {
            continue
        }
        if n ≻ 3 {
            break
        }
        print n
    }
}

A loop can also carry its own error handler — see catch attaches to more than do.

Thread loops#

A loop marked thread (la thread) runs its iterations as independent lanes: for from src at [i, j] thread lane let v { … }. Because the lanes run independently, one lane cannot stop the others. continue skips the rest of this lane, but break is SEM010 break_in_thread_body and a plain return is SEM010 return_in_thread_body. To use a lane's own stores, write only that lane's coordinate; a loop whose independence the compiler cannot prove is SEM010 filum_independence_unproven.

return thread (la return thread) ends the current lane from any depth of the lane body's own blocks. It takes no value, because lanes deliver results through their stores. Anywhere else it is refused: outside a thread loop (SEM010 return_thread_outside_lane), with a value (SEM010 return_thread_with_value), or inside a nested closure or reduction body (SEM010 return_thread_in_nested_body).

kernel lane_exit(tensor<f32, [4]> values) → void {
    for from values at [i] thread lane let value {
        return thread
    }
}
fn run() → void {
    return thread
}

main {
    run()
}

Known issue in 1.19: return thread is checked but not yet compiled. The code generators and the lowering to the runner's form refuse it by name (return_thread_lowering_pending), so a program that uses it passes `faber check and stops at faber check --lower, faber build and faber run`. The formatter keeps it as written.
